chapter: The Playbook for Building a Multimillion-Dollar SaaS
idea: Bootstrapping is a focus decision: defaulting to the best-business model, best business fits the founder — benefits of ownership, speed, and staying small-but-profitable.
application: For side-project tasks, bias toward the smallest experiment that can validate demand before building machinery around it.

chapter: Achieving Escape Velocity
idea: Escape velocity for SaaS means self-sustaining growth — every system should aim to reduce founder-dependent surface area.
application: Flag tasks that create manual maintenance (hand-run pipelines) as candidates for automation follow-ups.

chapter: Market — Strengthening Product-Market Fit
idea: Product-market fit precedes growth: scale amplifies whatever is there, so fix fit before pouring on marketing.
application: Before scheduling 'add features' tasks, schedule evidence-gathering (user conversations, usage analysis) first.

chapter: Market — How Much Should I Worry about Competition?
idea: Competitive advantage comes from narrow niches and accumulated insight, not from building more features than rivals.
application: In capture, features that competitors also have are weak bets; propose the ones tied to the user's unique distribution or insight.

chapter: Market — How Can I Build a Moat?
idea: Great moats in bootstrapped SaaS are integrations, community, and switching costs — small emphases that compound into defensibility.
application: When proposing roadmap work, prefer items that deepen lock-in or community value over one-off feature parity.

chapter: Pricing — How Should I Structure My Pricing?
idea: Pricing should be understandable, segment-aligned, and leave room to grow with the customer's value.
application: When building pricing-related features (plans, gates), implement the simplest structure that captures segment differences.

chapter: Pricing — SaaS Cheat Code: Expansion Revenue
idea: Expansion revenue (customers paying more as they grow) beats constant new-customer acquisition for compounding MRR.
application: Track and task retention-side work (upgrades, power-user paths) with the same rigor as new-feature work.

chapter: Pricing — Should I Ask for a Credit Card Up Front?
idea: Asking for payment up front filters customers to those with real intent; free access attracts evaluators, not buyers.
application: In experiments around onboarding or trials, bias toward friction that tests genuine intent rather than vanity signups.

chapter: Pricing — When Should I Raise Prices?
idea: Raise prices early and often: doing it with few customers is a smaller fire to manage and signals real value delivery.
application: For growth items like pricing changes, schedule explicit 'communicate change' prep — value justification comes before the request.

chapter: Marketing — How Do I Find More Customers?
idea: Marketing is a search problem: figure out where your best customers already hang out and test small, parallel channels.
application: Turning big marketing goals into small test campaigns with success criteria beats 'do more marketing' as a task.

chapter: Marketing — Marketing Funnels / Dual Funnels
idea: Map the funnel explicitly and optimize one stage at a time; conversion dominates traffic quality for durable growth.
application: Break marketing tracing into concrete per-stage tasks (fix onboarding first vs drive traffic first) instead of vague growth pushes.

chapter: Team — How Should I Structure My Team?
idea: Early-stage SaaS ships best with a small core of generalists and critical hires made sequential — not a broad team too soon.
application: In staffing or collaboration tasks, prefer minimal roles with clear owners over committees; every meeting needs an owner with a decision.

chapter: Team — How Can I Hire Great People?
idea: Hire for attitude + aptitude; paying attention to agency (ownership) filters better than pedigree-based signals.
application: For interview-related tasks, weigh behavioral signals of agency alongside technical drills.

chapter: 80/20 SaaS Metrics — Which Metrics Should I Track?
idea: Track a handful of high-leverage metrics (new MRR, churn, burn runway); ignore the noise metrics that don't drive decisions.
application: In reviews and briefs, prefer few decision-driving numbers over dashboards; skip vanity metrics unless they set next action.

chapter: Metrics — 3 High/3 Low Metrics Framework
idea: Three high / three low: regularly review what's going best and worst, and generate action items from each extreme.
application: Emulate this framing in weekly reviews — surface both 'working' and 'stalling' patterns and translate them into concrete tasks.

chapter: Metrics — How Much Should I Worry about Churn?
idea: Churn compounds silently; treating it as a numbers-only problem misses the retention conversations and product gaps behind it.
application: When metrics show regression, propose the diagnostic task (investigate X) instead of reflexively scheduling feature work.

chapter: Metrics — SaaS Cheat Code: Net Negative Churn
idea: Net negative churn means revenue grows even with some cancelation — maximizing customer success pays like new sales.
application: When building features for power users, weight the ones that continue delivering value (habit loops) over one-time wins.

chapter: Mindset — Where Should I Focus My Time?
idea: Founders' time follows an 80/20: a few activities (product, audience) create most movement — say no to the rest.
application: When the matrix crowds with small urgencies, invoke this principle to shed low-yield commitments the user can decline.

chapter: Mindset — Am I Turning Speed Bumps into Roadblocks?
idea: Most startup problems are speed bumps — recoverable with persistence — not roadblocks; panic escalates bumps into walls.
application: When a capture reads as a blocker, ask if it's actually a bump with a dated small fix rather than a full stop.

chapter: Mindset — How Can I Avoid Burnout?
idea: Burnout comes from unbounded ambition plus no finish lines; deliberate rest and predictable hours are performance infrastructure.
application: Watch for overfull weeks in the weekly review — propose a sustainable cadence: scheduled evening guard and at least one full day off.
